questions.q: State the Principle of Mathematical Induction precisely, naming the two required conditions and the conclusion.
questions.a: Correct answer: Let P(n) be a statement involving natural number n. If (i) P(1) is true, and (ii) for every k ∈ ℕ, P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) is true, then P(n) is true for all n ∈ ℕ. A wrong answer revealing "checking P(1), P(2), P(3) is enough" shows the student confuses inductive reasoning (pattern spotting) with mathematical induction (deductive proof). Another error: omitting "for an arbitrary k" in the inductive step, indicating they don't grasp the universal quantifier's role.

questions.q: A student claims: "I checked the formula 1+2+...+n = n(n+1)/2 for n=1,2,3,4,5 and it worked every time. Therefore it is true for all n." Explain why this argument is mathematically insufficient, referencing the difference between empirical verification and deductive proof.
questions.a: Correct answer: Checking finitely many cases (even a million) never proves a statement for infinitely many natural numbers; a counterexample could exist at n=6 or n=10⁶+1. Mathematical induction provides a logical chain covering all n in one argument. A wrong answer like "it's sufficient because the pattern is obvious" reveals the student hasn't internalised that mathematics requires proof beyond pattern recognition — a critical shift from Class 10 empirical approaches to Class 11 rigour.

questions.q: Consider the statement P(n): "n² + n + 41 is prime for all n ∈ ℕ." Identify the base case P(1) and the inductive hypothesis P(k) that would be assumed in an induction proof attempt. Do not attempt the inductive step.
questions.a: Correct answer: Base case P(1): 1² + 1 + 41 = 43, which is prime. Inductive hypothesis P(k): Assume k² + k + 41 is prime for some arbitrary k ∈ ℕ. A wrong answer writing P(k) as "for all k" instead of "for some arbitrary k" shows confusion between universal statement and inductive assumption. Another error: trying to prove P(k) rather than assuming it, indicating they don't understand the hypothetical nature of the inductive hypothesis.

questions.q: Compare the logical structure of proving "∑_{i=1}^n i = n(n+1)/2" by (a) direct derivation using the Gaussian pairing method, and (b) mathematical induction. Which method assumes the formula beforehand? Which method discovers the formula? Explain the epistemological difference.
questions.a: Correct answer: Gaussian pairing derives the formula without knowing it in advance (discovery); induction verifies a conjectured formula (verification). Induction requires the formula as input; direct derivation produces it. A wrong answer claiming "both are the same" or "induction discovers the formula" reveals the student doesn't distinguish between proof of a known statement and derivation of an unknown one — a nuance critical for board exam "prove by induction" vs "find and prove" questions.

questions.q: A faulty induction proof claims: "All horses are the same colour. Base case: 1 horse has same colour. Inductive step: Assume any k horses have same colour. For k+1 horses, remove one — remaining k have same colour by hypothesis. Put it back, remove a different one — those k have same colour. Therefore all k+1 have same colour." Identify the exact logical flaw and the smallest k where the argument breaks.
questions.a: Correct answer: The flaw is in the transition from k=1 to k=2. The two subsets of k horses (after removing different horses) have no overlap when k=1, so the "same colour" property cannot be transferred. The argument implicitly assumes k ≥ 2. A wrong answer pointing to "base case is wrong" or "inductive hypothesis is false" shows the student cannot analyse the structural dependency between base case and inductive step — a classic senior-secondary error in evaluating induction validity.

questions.q: Construct a statement P(n) about natural numbers that is true for n=1,2,3,4,5 but false for n=6, demonstrating why finite verification fails. Explain how mathematical induction would prevent accepting this false statement.
questions.a: Correct answer: Example: P(n): "n² - 7n + 13 is prime." True for n=1..5 (values: 7, 3, 1, 1, 3 — all prime if we consider 1 as prime, or adjust to n² - 5n + 7 giving 3, 1, 1, 3, 7). Better: P(n): "n! < n³" true for n=1..5, false at n=6 (720 > 216). Induction would fail at the inductive step when trying to prove P(5) ⇒ P(6), exposing the falsehood. A poor answer giving a statement false at n=1 or n=2 shows the student doesn't understand the requirement that base case must hold for the counterexample to illustrate the limitation of finite checking.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ induction is a deductive proof technique used to establish that a statement P(n) holds for every natural number n ∈ ℕ.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are ______ at the bottom of the infinite staircase of the Qutub Minar.
What is Mathematical induction? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Mathematical induction is a deductive proof technique used to establish that a statement P(n) holds for every natural number n ∈ ℕ.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: You don't climb each step to check; instead, you prove two things: (______) You can step onto the first step (base case).
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Mathematical induction?
questions.a: Students treat the inductive hypothesis as "P(k) is true for all k" rather than "P(k) is true for some arbitrary but fixed k".

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can articulate the two-step structure of mathematical induction in their own words, correctly identify the base case and inductive hypothesis in a given proof framework, and explain why the "domino effect" analogy logically guarantees truth for all natural numbers without checking each case individually.
